opus-5.5.text:
That's a really good question, and I think it's one people don't talk about enough.

Data scarcity isn't just a bottleneck on its own. It also hides the other bottlenecks. In robotics we're in a regime where we simply don't have enough data, nowhere near the internet-scale data language models enjoy. So whenever a model fails, the easiest explanation, and often the correct one, is "we need more data." That makes it hard to tell whether something else is also holding us back.

Take architecture. Is the transformer-based policy we're using the right one for robotics? Do we need a better action representation, better handling of high-frequency control, or better ways to fuse vision, language and proprioception? Or take the learning objective: is imitation learning enough, or do we need reinforcement learning on top? When you're data-starved, all of these questions get muddied. You run an experiment, you change the architecture, and you see a small difference. But you don't know whether that difference will hold, shrink or reverse once you have ten or a hundred times more data. Many tricks that help in the low-data regime turn out not to matter at scale, and things that look useless at small scale can become important later.

So in a sense, data scarcity puts a fog over the whole field. In language modeling, once people had abundant data, they could run clean scaling-law studies and isolate what actually mattered: model size, compute, data quality. In robotics we can't do that cleanly yet, so a lot of our intuitions about what the "real" bottlenecks are remain somewhat speculative.

That's one reason I'm excited about anything that makes data cheaper: simulation, learning from human videos, more scalable teleoperation, and getting robots deployed so they collect data in the real world. It's not only about making models better directly. Once we're past the data bottleneck, or at least once it's less severe, we'll finally see clearly what the next bottleneck is. My guess is it may be things like long-horizon reasoning, reliability, or the gap between perception and precise physical interaction. But honestly, right now it's hard to be sure, because data dominates everything.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics has far less data than language models and that data dominates, but does not state that current data volumes are insufficient to saturate models’ capabilities.

r002.rationale: The response says data scarcity hides other bottlenecks and that the next bottleneck will become clear once the data bottleneck is less severe.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a really good question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot. The short answer is that data scarcity doesn't just limit performance, it actually obscures everything else. It's like trying to debug a system when the main variable is maxed out in the wrong direction.

Let me explain what I mean. In language models, you had this massive corpus from the internet, and once you had that, you could run very clean experiments. You could ask, is the architecture the bottleneck? Is it compute? Is it the training objective? And you could isolate those because data was not the thing holding you back. In robotics we don't have that luxury. When a robot policy fails, I often genuinely cannot tell you whether it failed because the model is too small, because the architecture is wrong for the problem, because the action representation is bad, or simply because it never saw anything remotely like that situation in training. All of those produce the same symptom, which is the robot does something dumb.

So data scarcity acts as a kind of fog. Every other bottleneck is hiding behind it. When we tried scaling up models, for example, we sometimes saw very modest gains, and the tempting conclusion is that scaling doesn't work for robotics. But I think the more honest conclusion is that we were data-starved, so a bigger model just had more capacity to memorize the same small dataset. You can't learn anything about scaling laws if you're not in the regime where scaling is meaningful.

There's a second effect too, which is that scarcity forces design decisions early that then get baked in. Because real robot data is so expensive, people lean on simulation, on human video, on cross-embodiment data. Each of those introduces its own gap, sim-to-real, embodiment mismatch, missing proprioception. So now when something doesn't work, you have an additional layer of confounders stacked on top. Was it the model, or was it the domain gap in the data you used to compensate for not having real data?

What I've found helpful is to be very deliberate about building small controlled settings where data is actually not the constraint, even if the task is narrow. Pick one task, collect more demonstrations than you think you need, and then push on the other axes. That's where you can start to see things like, oh, actually the action chunking matters a lot here, or the visual encoder is the real limitation, or the policy is fine but inference latency is killing us. Those insights are hard to get when everything is confounded by not having enough data.

And then the last thing I'd say, and this is somewhat optimistic, is that as the community collectively gets more data, through larger shared datasets, through better simulation, through more robots in the world, I expect a lot of the other bottlenecks to suddenly become visible all at once. We'll probably discover that several of our assumptions about architecture and training were really just artifacts of the data regime we were in. So I think data scarcity is the first bottleneck not just in importance, but in the sense that it has to be cleared before you can properly see the rest.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics is data-starved and that larger models can only memorize the same small dataset, so scaling is not meaningful. This communicates that current data volumes are insufficient to use the models’ capacity.

r002.rationale: The response says data scarcity obscures other bottlenecks and makes it impossible to tell whether failures come from model size, architecture, action representation, or missing training examples.

astra-6.text:
I think data scarcity can actually hide other bottlenecks. If a model doesn’t perform well, it’s hard to tell whether the problem is the architecture, the training objective, or simply that it hasn’t seen enough relevant experience. You might spend a lot of time improving the model when what it really needs is more diverse data.

And in robotics, it’s not just the amount of data. You need coverage of different environments, objects, and failures. If your data only contains successful demonstrations in a narrow setting, you may never discover the limitations that matter when the robot operates somewhere new.

So I would treat collecting data and identifying bottlenecks as an iterative process. Expand the data, measure which failures improve and which persist, and use that to guide the next experiment. You don’t have to solve data scarcity completely, but you need enough controlled variation to separate a data problem from a model problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how limited and narrow data can obscure model problems, but it does not state that current robotics data volumes are insufficient to saturate model capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says data scarcity can hide other bottlenecks and make it hard to tell whether poor performance comes from the architecture, training objective, or lack of relevant experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data scarcity makes it difficult to know what the next bottleneck really is. If a model doesn’t perform well, is it because the architecture isn’t capable enough, or because it simply hasn’t seen enough examples? In robotics, those two things are often tangled together.

For example, if a robot fails to grasp an unfamiliar object, we might need a better model, but we might also just need more diverse training data. Until we can test those possibilities systematically, we risk spending a lot of effort fixing the wrong thing.

So collecting more data isn’t only about improving performance. It also helps us diagnose the system. As we increase the amount and diversity of data, we can see which failures go away and which persist. Those persistent failures give us a clearer picture of where the other bottlenecks are.

r001.rationale: The response says more and more diverse data can improve diagnosis, but does not state that current data volumes are insufficient to saturate model capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says data scarcity makes it difficult to know what the next bottleneck is and risks fixing the wrong thing, directly communicating that scarcity hinders identifying it.
